lessons.title: Atomic Structure
lessons.objective: Distinguish atoms, molecules and ions, state the contributions of Dalton, Millikan, Rutherford, Moseley, Thomson and Bohr, count protons/neutrons/electrons from atomic and mass numbers, name the four quantum numbers and the rules for filling orbitals, describe s and p orbital shapes, and calculate relative atomic mass from isotopes.

content.heading: Atomic Structure
paragraphs: You have touched atoms all your life without seeing one. They are the tiny beads behind everything: your phone, your food, your chemistry textbook, you. This lesson gives you names for the three shapes those beads come in, and a simple way to count the parts inside them.

content.heading: Atoms, molecules and ions in daily words
paragraphs: Think of an atom as one single grain of an element, like one grain of rice. Join some grains together and you get a molecule: atoms holding hands. Take a grain and give or remove an electron, and it picks up a charge, becoming an ion.

Protons are positive, and neutrons are neutral. H and He are atoms; H{{sub:2O}} is a molecule; Na{{sup:+}} is an ion. The story of how we found these pieces goes like this: Dalton proposed indivisible atoms combining in whole-number ratios, Thomson discovered the electron in cathode rays, Rutherford’s gold foil showed the nucleus is tiny, Moseley’s X-rays proved atomic number decides identity, Millikan’s oil drop measured the charge e, and Bohr placed electrons in shells to explain spectral lines.
bullets: Atom: one grain. Molecule: grains holding hands. Ion: a grain carrying charge.
Dalton atoms; Thomson electron from cathode rays; Rutherford nucleus from gold foil; Moseley Z from X-rays; Millikan charge e; Bohr shells for spectral lines.
content.takeaway: Atoms are single grains, molecules are joined grains and ions carry a charge.

check.question: Which statement correctly tells the three particles apart?
options: Na is a molecule, Na+ is an atom and NaCl is an ion
Na is an atom, Na+ is an ion and NaCl is a formula unit of a compound
Na is an ion, Na+ is a molecule and NaCl is an atom
Na, Na+ and NaCl are all molecules
check.why: Na is one atom, Na+ is that atom minus one electron, and NaCl is a formula unit, not a standalone molecule.

content.heading: Counting the three parts of an atom
paragraphs: Picture the atom as a class of people. The proton count is the element’s name tag. That count is the atomic number, Z. Add the neutrons to the protons and you get the mass number, A. For a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals Z.

Neutrons are simply whatever is left: neutrons equal A minus Z. Chlorine has Z = 17, so 17 protons and normally 17 electrons. Isotopes are family members that differ only in neutrons, like {{sup:35}}Cl and {{sup:37}}Cl. The relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average: (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) ÷ 100 = 35.5.
bullets: Z = protons = the element’s identity.
Neutrons = A − Z; electrons = Z when the atom is neutral.
RAM weighs each isotope by abundance, never a plain average.
content.takeaway: Z counts protons, A − Z counts neutrons and abundance sets the average.

check.question: For 37Cl, how many protons and neutrons does one atom contain?
check.why: Chlorine has Z = 17, so protons = 17 and neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20.

content.heading: Shells, addresses and shapes
paragraphs: Electrons live on floors (shells) around the nucleus, inside orbitals. Four quantum numbers address each electron: n floor, l room type, ml exact room, ms spin.
Three rules govern how the rooms fill. Aufbau fills the lowest rooms first. Hund spreads electrons singly before pairing them. Pauli allows two per room, spinning opposite ways.

An s orbital is a round cloud holding 2 electrons. A p subshell is three dumbbells holding 6. Chlorine (Z = 17) arranges as 1s{{sup:2}} 2s{{sup:2}} 2p{{sup:6}} 3s{{sup:2}} 3p{{sup:5}}. Count them: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17. From Z = 1 to 20 the table runs H (1s{{sup:1}}) up to Ca (1s{{sup:2}} 2s{{sup:2}} 2p{{sup:6}} 3s{{sup:2}} 3p{{sup:6}} 4s{{sup:2}}), filling shells 1 to 3 before 4s.
bullets: Shells are floors; orbitals are rooms; quantum numbers are addresses.
Aufbau: lowest first. Hund: singly first. Pauli: two at most.
s = round cloud (2); p = three dumbbells (6).
Z 1–20: H 1s{{sup:1}} to Ca 2,8,8,2. Add superscripts, check against Z.
content.takeaway: Four quantum numbers address each electron and three rules govern filling.

check.question: Which set respects the Pauli principle for two electrons?
options: 1s2 with ms = +{{frac:1|2}} and -{{frac:1|2}} in the same orbital
1s3 with three electrons in one orbital
2p6 with all six electrons paired in one orbital
check.why: Pauli allows at most two electrons per orbital, and they must spin in opposite directions.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why mass number and atomic number differ
paragraphs: Atomic number Z and mass number A answer different questions. Z asks what element it is: the proton count decides the family. A asks how heavy the atom is: protons plus neutrons. Two atoms can share the same Z and still carry different A values, and that is exactly what isotopes are.

Chlorine shows the pair: {{sup:35}}Cl and {{sup:37}}Cl both have Z = 17 but they differ in neutrons (18 versus 20). Calcium-40 and argon-40 show the reverse case: the same A = 40 but different Z values (20 versus 18), so they are different elements with the same mass.

That is why the periodic table is ordered by Z and not by A. Moseley’s X-ray work showed that Z fixes identity, and the odd mass-order inversion (argon before potassium) disappears once Z takes over. Mass decides the average weight; proton count decides identity.

A useful habit: read the numbers in order (top number A, bottom number Z in the usual symbol) and ask first what Z tells you, then what A adds. Most isotope errors come from treating the two numbers as one idea.
bullets: Z = identity; A = weight; they are not the same idea.
Same Z, different A = isotopes; same A, different Z = different elements.
The table is ordered by Z (Moseley), not by mass.
Read Z first, then ask what A adds.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the octet is stable
paragraphs: Atoms behave like small rooms whose outer shell wants eight electrons: the octet. Sodium (2,8,1) carries one electron in its outer shell and loses it to become Na{{sup:+}} with a full (2,8) shell, which is why sodium reacts so eagerly. Chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to reach Cl{{sup:-}} (2,8,8), completing its octet.

Helium is the exception that proves the rule: its shell holds only two electrons (1s{{sup:2}}), the duet, and it is completely inert. Noble gases are inert because their outer shells are already full, and other atoms become stable by matching that arrangement.

This one idea predicts bonding and ion formation. Elements on the left of the table lose electrons to reach a full shell; elements on the right gain them. Hydrogen and helium are the only elements that stop at two.

The octet also explains why metals conduct electricity and why some compounds form lattice structures: ions with full shells pack stably. Every later lesson on bonding leans on this idea, so it is worth understanding before you move on.
bullets: Outer shell wants 8 electrons (octet); helium wants 2 (duet).
Na loses 1 to fill its shell; Cl gains 1 to fill its own.
Reached-octet atoms are stable and unreactive.
Bonding predictions start from this rule.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in atomic structure
paragraphs: The commonest trap is swapping the two numbers: writing A as the proton count or Z as the mass. The question ‘how many protons in {{sup:40}}_2{{sub:0Ca}}?’ tests exactly that: 20, from Z, not 40. Always hunt for Z first.

The second trap is taking a plain average of isotope masses. The RAM of chlorine is not (35 + 37) ÷ 2 = 36; it is abundance-weighted and equals 35.5. Averages in chemistry are weighted by how common each part is.

The third trap is electron counting for ions. Na{{sup:+}} has 10 electrons, not 11, because losing one electron changes only the electron count; Z and A stay put. Cl{{sup:-}} has 18 electrons for the same reason in reverse.

The fourth trap is configuration totals. After you write a configuration, add the superscripts and check the sum against Z. A sum that does not match Z means the arrangement is wrong, no matter how neatly it looks.
bullets: Protons come from Z, never from A.
RAM is abundance-weighted, not a plain average.
Ions change electron count only; Z and A stay fixed.
Check configuration totals against Z every time.

lessons.title: Chemical Combination
lessons.objective: State the laws of definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions and conservation of mass, write chemical symbols, formulae and balanced equations, and perform mole-concept calculations (moles from mass, concentration, gas volume) and stoichiometry.

content.heading: Chemical Combination
paragraphs: If moles ever felt like a foreign language, you are not alone. Here is the reassuring part: chemicals combine in fixed, weighable amounts, like rice weighed on a trader's scale. This lesson shows you the three laws behind those amounts, and how counting by weighing actually works.

content.heading: Three laws in plain words
paragraphs: Conservation of mass says matter is rearranged, never created or destroyed. 12 g carbon plus 32 g oxygen gives 44 g carbon dioxide (12 + 32 = 44).
Definite proportions says a compound always keeps the same mass ratio. Water is always 1 g hydrogen to 8 g oxygen. A changed ratio means a different compound.

Multiple proportions says that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple ratio. 12 g carbon uses 16 g oxygen in CO and 32 g in CO{{sub:2}}: a ratio of 1:2.

Reciprocal proportions say that the masses of two elements combining with a fixed mass of a third are in a simple ratio. With 8 g oxygen combining with 1 g hydrogen and 3 g carbon, hydrogen and carbon combine as 1:3.
bullets: Mass in equals mass out.
Compounds keep fixed mass ratios.
Paired compounds use simple ratios.
Reciprocal links ratios through a fixed third element.
content.takeaway: Mass is conserved; ratios are fixed and simple.

check.question: 12 g of carbon forms CO with 16 g of oxygen and CO{{sub:2}} with 32 g. Which law do 16 and 32 illustrate?
check.why: For a fixed mass of carbon, the oxygen masses 16 and 32 sit in the simple ratio 1:2.

content.heading: Formulae and balanced equations
paragraphs: A formula counts atoms: H{{sub:2O}} means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Writing the formula is writing the recipe.
Symbols form a system: one letter for H, O and C, two for Na and Cl. The first letter is capital, the second small, so Co is cobalt but CO is carbon plus oxygen.

A balanced equation has equal atom counts on both sides, since atoms are only rearranged. CH{{sub:4}} + 2O{{sub:2}} → CO{{sub:2}} + 2H{{sub:2O}} has C1 H4 O4 on both sides. If the counts differ, the equation lies about conservation.
Percentage composition gives the empirical formula: divide each percentage by its Ar, then by the smallest value. A compound of 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O gives 3.3, 6.7, 3.3 → CH{{sub:2O}}.
bullets: A formula counts atoms; subscripts are counts.
Symbols: H, O are one letter; Na, Cl two; Co ≠ CO.
Balancing means equal atom counts on both sides.
Percentage composition gives the empirical formula.
content.takeaway: Formulae count atoms, equations must balance and percentages become formulae.

check.question: A compound is 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
check.why: Dividing by Ar (12, 1, 16) gives 3.3, 6.7, 3.3, so the ratio is 1:2:1.

content.heading: The mole: counting by weighing
paragraphs: One mole is a counting unit, just like a dozen eggs: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10{{sup:23}} particles. A mole of any substance carries the same count, only the masses differ.
Moles = mass ÷ Mr (relative molecular mass). Methane (Mr = 16): 0.5 mol = 8 g; one mole fills 22.4 dm{{sup:3}} at s.t.p.; concentration = moles ÷ volume.
Stoichiometry applies the equation's mole ratio. Calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) gives one mole of CO{{sub:2}} per mole, so 50 g is 0.5 mol releasing 11.2 dm{{sup:3}} at s.t.p.

Relative atomic mass is measured against carbon-12: {{sup:12}}C is assigned exactly 12. The relative mass of any atom is the average mass of its isotopes compared with one twelfth of a {{sup:12}}C atom. That standard lets Ar and Mr be linked by weighing.
bullets: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10{{sup:23}} particles.
Moles = mass ÷ Mr; gas = 22.4 dm{{sup:3}} per mole.
Stoichiometry applies the equation's mole ratio.
{{sup:12}}C = 12 exactly is the scale for Ar and Mr.
content.takeaway: A mole counts particles by weighing them.

check.question: What is the mass of 0.5 mol of methane, CH{{sub:4}} (Mr = 16)?
check.why: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.5 × 16 = 8 g.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Changed a unit mid-question? Convert cm{{sup:3}} to dm{{sup:3}} first (divide by 1000). Most mole errors in the exam hall are unit errors, not concept errors.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why equations must balance
paragraphs: An equation is a balance: the atoms on the left must equal the atoms on the right, because reactions only rearrange. Unbalanced equations pretend atoms appear or vanish, which breaks conservation of mass. Balancing is counting, not decoration.

The counting order that never fails: balance metals first, then non-metals, then oxygen and hydrogen last. Metals rarely appear more than once per side, while oxygen and hydrogen hide inside several compounds and need a final check.

In CH{{sub:4}} + 2O{{sub:2}} → CO{{sub:2}} + 2H{{sub:2O}} the carbon balances at once, hydrogen forces 2H{{sub:2O}}, and oxygen then forces 2O{{sub:2}}. Notice the coefficients: doubling the H{{sub:2O}} also doubles its oxygen, which is why oxygen is adjusted last.

A reliable habit is to count each element across the whole arrow, not per compound. Total counts, not written counts, decide balance; that is the habit that stops a balanced-looking equation from being wrong.
Count totals before you adjust coefficients and you will balance almost every equation on the first attempt. It costs you seconds and saves whole marks.
The same system explains why fractional coefficients get tidied by multiplying the whole equation through: the atom totals do not change, only the presentation does.
bullets: Balancing is counting: atoms are only rearranged.
Order: metals, non-metals, then oxygen and hydrogen.
Count totals across the whole arrow, not inside one compound.

content.heading: Go deeper: Empirical and molecular formulae compared
paragraphs: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is the true count in one molecule. Glucose and fructose share the empirical formula CH{{sub:2O}}, but only glucose is written C{{sub:6H}}{{sub:1}}{{sub:2O}}{{sub:6}}. The ratio is the same; the size is not.

The link between them is the molar mass. CH{{sub:2O}} has Mr = 30 and glucose has Mr = 180, so 180 ÷ 30 = 6, meaning the true formula is six empirical units. Comparing Mr values converts one formula into the other without any new experiment.

Finding an empirical formula is the reverse journey: percentage composition gives the atom ratio directly, and a measured Mr then scales the ratio up to the molecular formula. Percentages alone can never give the true formula; they only give the ratio.
The exam trap is to stop at the ratio when a molar mass was given. If Mr appears anywhere in the question, the answer needs scaling. No Mr, no scaling: that is the whole discrimination.
Empirical formulae also predict percentage composition, so you can move in either direction between ratio, percentages and true formula in one set of steps.
bullets: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = true count.
Scale the ratio by Mr ÷ empirical Mr.
Percentages alone never give the molecular formula.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in mole calculations
paragraphs: The first trap is confusing Mr with relative atomic mass: Mr is for a molecule, Ar for an atom. Water's Mr is 18 (2 × 1 + 16), while oxygen's Ar is 16. Use the wrong one and every mole count after it goes wrong.

The second trap is skipping the ratio. Two moles of acid may need only one mole of base; multiplying by the equation's ratio comes before any concentration arithmetic. Which reactant is limiting comes from the smaller mole count after dividing by the coefficients.

The third trap is s.t.p. values quoted at the wrong temperature. The 22.4 dm{{sup:3}} molar volume belongs to 273 K and 1 atm; at any other temperature you must use the gas law, not the memorised volume.

The fourth trap is unit mixing: cm{{sup:3}} against dm{{sup:3}}, or grammes against kilograms. Moles ÷ volume needs dm{{sup:3}}, and examiners plant cm{{sup:3}} figures precisely to catch anyone who skips the conversion. Convert first, calculate second. Always.
Reading the question twice catches the last trap: write the units beside every number as you work, and that habit will expose mismatches before they cost you marks.
bullets: Mr is per molecule; Ar is per atom.
Apply the equation ratio before concentrations.
22.4 dm{{sup:3}} belongs only to 273 K and 1 atm.
Convert cm{{sup:3}} to dm{{sup:3}} before dividing.

lessons.title: Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas
lessons.objective: Apply kinetic theory to distinguish solids, liquids and gases, explain changes of state and Brownian movement, deduce the gas laws from their statements, use the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and vapour density, and state factors that make real gases deviate from ideal.

content.heading: Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas
paragraphs: Steam rising off a pot of hot yam water, smoke drifting across a food stall: both are invisible particles in motion. If gas laws ever felt like a list to memorise, here is the secret. The movement of tiny particles explains every law in this lesson, and you can picture each one.

content.heading: Particles in motion make solids, liquids and gases
paragraphs: Everything is made of particles that are always moving. Solids vibrate in fixed positions, liquids slide past each other, and gases move freely to fill a room. Particle speed and freedom set the state.
Melting lets particles slip past each other. Boiling lets them escape from everywhere at once. Vapourisation escapes only from the surface, at any temperature.
Freezing locks particles in place; condensation returns a gas to a liquid. Brownian movement proves it: smoke jiggles as invisible air particles bump it.

Gases differ in atomicity: the atoms per molecule in one formula unit. Helium is monatomic (He), hydrogen and oxygen diatomic (H{{sub:2}}, O{{sub:2}}), and carbon dioxide polyatomic (CO{{sub:2}}). Atomicity changes molar mass and diffusion, so H{{sub:2}} diffuses faster than O{{sub:2}}.
bullets: Solids vibrate in place; liquids slide; gases move freely.
Boiling bubbles throughout; vapourisation escapes only from the surface.
Brownian movement shows invisible particles bumping visible ones.
Monatomic He; diatomic H{{sub:2}}, O{{sub:2}}; polyatomic CO{{sub:2}}.
content.takeaway: The speed of particles decides whether matter is solid, liquid or gas.

check.question: A puddle dries on a cool day without ever bubbling. Which change is this?
check.why: Vapourisation is escape from the surface at any temperature; boiling bubbles throughout.

visual.caption: Heating speeds particles, so they escape fixed places, slide past each other, then fly freely.

content.heading: Six gas laws in daily words
paragraphs: Boyle's law says squeezing a gas raises its pressure, like crowding a bus. Charles's law says a gas grows when heated, because faster particles push harder. Gay-Lussac's law says pressure rises with temperature in a sealed container.

Avogadro's law says equal volumes hold equal numbers: one mole fills 22.4 dm{{sup:3}} at s.t.p. Graham's law says light gases diffuse faster by the √Mr ratio. Dalton's law adds each gas's pressure in a mixture.
Each law holds one variable constant, so read that constant first.
Boyle is a P–V hyperbola; Charles is a V–T straight line through 0 K; Gay-Lussac is P–T through the same point. Read the constant first; the shape tells you the law.
bullets: Boyle: squeeze a gas and pressure rises.
Charles: heat a gas and volume rises (in kelvin).
Avogadro: equal volumes, equal numbers. Graham: light is faster. Dalton: pressures add.
content.takeaway: Pressure, volume and temperature trade off in fixed, predictable ways.

check.question: A gas is squeezed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?
check.why: Boyle's law says P ∝ 1/V, so halving V doubles P at constant temperature.

visual.caption: Boyle's law is a hyperbola: half the volume doubles the pressure.

content.heading: One equation that joins them
paragraphs: The ideal gas equation joins all the laws together: PV = nRT. P is pressure, V is volume, n is moles, T is temperature in kelvin, and R is a constant. Pressure × volume equals amount × temperature.
One mole occupies 22.4 dm{{sup:3}} at 273 K and 1 atm (the molar volume). Vapour density is Mr ÷ 2, so a vapour density of 16 means Mr = 32. That converts a gas measurement into a mass.

Real gases misbehave at high pressure and low temperature. An ideal gas is the strict rule; a real gas is the rule with exceptions. The two factors behind the deviation are the finite size of the molecules and the forces between them.
bullets: PV = nRT joins pressure, volume, amount and temperature.
One mole fills 22.4 dm{{sup:3}} at s.t.p.; vapour density = Mr ÷ 2.
Deviation factors: finite molecular volume and intermolecular attractions, strongest at high P and low T.
content.takeaway: PV = nRT turns any two measurements into the rest.

check.question: What volume does 1 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 273 K and 1 atm?

visual.caption: Charles's law is a straight line through 0 K: 22.4 dm{{sup:3}} at 273 K for one mole.

Twice the temperature should double the volume from the worked example

content.heading: Go deeper: Why heating makes particles move faster
paragraphs: Temperature is the average speed of particles. Heating a gas hands energy to its particles, so the average speed rises. That is why Charles's law works: faster particles collide harder and push out to a larger volume.

The same idea explains boiling and vapourisation. At the surface, the fastest particles can escape at any temperature, which is vapourisation. Boiling needs the whole liquid to reach the energy where particles escape from everywhere, including bubbles inside.

It also explains why a gas's pressure climbs in a sealed container: the particles hit the walls harder and more often. Gay-Lussac's law is just Charles's law felt on the container instead of measured as volume.
Once you picture collisions instead of formulas, you can rebuild every gas law from this one image: speed makes pushing power, and pushing power is pressure.
The same picture explains why perfume spreads: the fastest molecules escape first and race across the room while the slower ones lag behind.
Cooling runs the film backwards, slowing particles until some can no longer escape and must condense.
bullets: Temperature measures average particle speed.
Heating raises speed, so gases expand.
Pressure is the force of particles hitting walls.
Pictures of collisions replace memorised laws.

content.heading: Go deeper: Graham's law worked case for hydrogen and oxygen
paragraphs: Graham's law says the rate of diffusion of a gas follows the inverse square root of its molar mass: rate ∝ 1 ÷ √Mr. Hydrogen (Mr = 2) against oxygen (Mr = 32) gives a rate ratio of √(32 ÷ 2) = √16 = 4, so hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster.

In time terms, if oxygen takes 40 seconds to diffuse the same distance, hydrogen takes 40 ÷ 4 = 10 seconds. The lighter gas always wins the race, which is why ammonia fumes cross a classroom long before heavier vapours even start.
The same ratio governs effusion through a tiny hole. A leaking balloon loses hydrogen fastest, not because hydrogen is ‘stronger’, but because its light particles move quicker between collisions.
The exam trap here is inverting the ratio. To correct it, ask first which gas is lighter; the lighter one must have the faster rate, so its number must come out larger.
bullets: Rate ratio = √(heavier Mr ÷ lighter Mr).
H{{sub:2}} diffuses 4× faster than O{{sub:2}} (√16 = 4).
The lighter gas always has the faster rate.
Effusion follows the same mass rule.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in gas calculations
paragraphs: The deadliest trap is temperature units. Charles's law and PV = nRT need kelvin; using Celsius compresses or stretches the answer by a huge factor. At 27 °C the correct temperature is 300 K, not 27, and that single slip re-scales every result by about eleven times.

The second trap is vapour density. Vapour density equals Mr ÷ 2, never Mr itself. A vapour density of 16 means a relative molecular mass of 32, not 16. The factor of two is the examiners' favourite silent divider.

The third trap forgets Boyle's condition. If pressure changes, Boyle's law cannot be applied until the temperature is confirmed constant. The question will always bury the condition in plain words like ‘the mixture is kept cool’.

The fourth trap is partial pressure addition in the wrong direction: Dalton's law adds pressures of separate gases sharing one container; it does not share one gas's pressure across gases. Reading ‘in the same vessel’ is the cue to add.
bullets: Always convert to kelvin (27 °C = 300 K).
Vapour density = Mr ÷ 2, never Mr.
Boyle's law needs constant temperature stated or implied.
Dalton's law adds gases sharing one vessel.

lessons.title: Periodic Table
lessons.objective: Relate atomic number to position on the periodic table, relate properties of groups of elements, explain variation of ionisation energy, ionic radii, electron affinity, electronegativity and conductivities across periods and down groups, and identify the alkali metals, alkaline-earth metals, halogens, noble gases and transition metals.

content.heading: Periodic Table
paragraphs: The periodic table can look like a wall chart full of tiny boxes, but it is actually a family album. The elements stand in columns because they share electrons the same way. Here is how to read the arrangement, and the trends it quietly hides.

content.heading: Rows, columns and families
paragraphs: The table reads by atomic number, the proton count. Each row, a period, fills one electron shell; each column, a group, holds elements sharing the same number of outer electrons. Sodium (Z = 11) sits in period 3.

Columns are families with shared behaviour. Group 1, the alkali metals, lose one electron easily. Group 2, the alkaline-earth metals, lose two. Group 17, the halogens, are non-metals that gain one electron. Group 18, the noble gases, are already full and almost never react.

Between the main blocks sit the transition metals, which form coloured compounds and work as catalysts. Their outer electrons sit in inner shells, so they can form several positive ions instead of just one or two.
bullets: Rows (periods) fill one electron shell each.
Columns (groups) share the number of outer electrons.
Group 1, 2, 17, 18 are alkali, alkaline-earth, halogens and nobles.
Transition metals form variable ions and coloured compounds.
content.takeaway: Same column means same outer electrons, and that means similar behaviour.

check.question: Which statement correctly pairs a family with its group?
check.why: Halogens sit in Group 17; the others are placed in different groups.

content.heading: Which way each property moves
paragraphs: Across a period, protons increase while electrons enter the same shell, so the electron pull grows. Atoms shrink, ionisation energy rises, electronegativity rises. Sodium yields to chlorine steadily, left to right.

Down a group, new shells are added outside, so atoms grow and the outer electrons are shielded from the nucleus. Ionisation energy and electronegativity fall, while metallic character grows. Fluorine, at the top of the halogens, is the most electronegative element of all.

Conductivity follows the same logic: metals conduct because outer electrons are free, and that freedom grows where atoms hold their electrons loosely. Thermal conductivity moves with electrical conductivity, since the same free electrons carry both heat and charge. Sodium conducts well; chlorine does not conduct at all.
bullets: Across a period: radius falls, ionisation energy and electronegativity rise.
Down a group: radius grows, ionisation energy and electronegativity fall.
Metallic character fades across and grows down.
Conductivity: electrical and thermal fall across the period, rise down the group.
content.takeaway: Across a period the pull grows; down a group new shells shield it.

visual.caption: More protons pull harder across; more shells shield better down.

check.question: Which order correctly arranges Na, Mg and Cl by electronegativity?
check.why: Electronegativity rises across the period, so Na < Mg < Cl.

content.heading: Why the trends happen
paragraphs: The root cause is a contest between nuclear charge and shielding. More protons pull harder, but more electron shells push the pull apart. Across a period, charge wins; down a group, shielding wins. Every trend on the table is that contest playing out.

Ionisation energy is the energy needed to pull an electron away. Across a period it rises because the pull grows; down a group it falls because shells shield the outer electron. The noble gases peak only where their full shells resist any change.

Ionic radius shrinks across a period, because the same electron shell is squeezed tighter. Going down, radius grows because each new shell adds a layer. Once you remember the contest, you can derive any trend without memorising a table.
bullets: Trends come from nuclear charge versus shielding.
Across: charge wins. Down: shielding wins.
Ionic radius follows the same contest.
Electron affinity rises across a period and falls down a group.
content.takeaway: Charge pulls in, shielding pushes out and the winner sets the trend.

check.question: Why does ionisation energy fall down a group?
options: Protons are fewer down the group
New shells are added, so outer electrons are shielded
Electrons are more numerous and pull harder
Atoms lose their neutrons down the group
check.why: Extra shells shield the nucleus, so outer electrons are held less tightly.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a trend question names two elements, first ask whether you are moving across or down. The direction decides everything before any values are compared.

content.problem: Arrange sodium, magnesium and chlorine in order of increasing electronegativity.

steps.reason: All sit in period 3: sodium first, magnesium second, chlorine third.
steps.result: Na, Mg, Cl left to right
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: Electronegativity rises left to right across a period. Best move: lean on the left-to-right trend, no memory required. If a group ever baffles you, count the shells. Closer to the nucleus means stronger pull.
steps.predictPrompt: What exactly does the question want you to write down first?

steps.reason: Sodium is the most metallic, chlorine the most electron-hungry.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

steps.reason: Electronegativity falls down a group: K < Na < Li.
steps.result: Trends run in both directions: up within a group, in across
steps.predictPrompt: Which way goes down the table?

steps.operation: Check to confirm: against Pauling values
steps.reason: Pauling values must rise Na < Mg < Cl; if one breaks the trend, the order slipped.
steps.result: Na 0.93, Mg 1.31, Cl 3.16: increasing as stated
steps.predictPrompt: Do the tabulated Pauling values keep that order?

content.problem: Arrange sodium, chlorine and oxygen in order of increasing first ionisation energy, and explain the order using the charge-versus-shielding argument.

steps.operation: Place the three in one row of the table
steps.reason: Na (period 3, group 1), O (period 2, group 16), Cl (period 3, group 17)
steps.result: so they share nearby positions and very different nuclear charges
steps.predictPrompt: Which two share a period, and which one sits above one of them?

steps.reason: across a period ionisation energy rises; down a group it falls
steps.result: O highest, Cl next, Na lowest
steps.predictPrompt: Why does the period position win here over the group?

steps.reason: Na holds only one 3s electron weakly; O and Cl hold outer electrons much tighter; O is one period up, so less shielding and still higher
steps.predictPrompt: Why does O beat Cl even though Cl has more protons?

steps.operation: Check to confirm: use the data
steps.reason: Na 496, Cl 1251, O 1314 kJ per mol — a widening gap consistent with the shielding argument
steps.result: the numbers match the order exactly
steps.predictPrompt: Do the values confirm the order, or overturn it?

content.question: Arrange fluorine, chlorine and bromine in order of increasing atomic radius, and say why.
hints: All three are halogens in one group
Count the electron shells in each atom
More shells means a larger atom

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionisation energy rises across but falls down
paragraphs: Ionisation energy is the toll paid to remove an electron. Across a period, each new proton is added to the same electron shell, so every electron feels a stronger pull. The toll therefore rises steadily from sodium to chlorine.

Down a group, each new element adds a whole shell outside the previous one. The outer electrons are not only farther away but shielded by inner shells, so the pull weakens and the toll falls. Potassium costs less to ionise than lithium for exactly this reason.
The trend pauses at the noble gases, whose full shells force a sudden jump in cost. That saw-tooth shape confirms the rule: shell structure, not mass alone, sets the price of removing an electron.
Explain the trend with charge-versus-shielding language and you earn the full mark; recite ‘it increases’ without the reason and you earn only part. The mechanism is the mark.
The same contest also sets electronegativity, electron affinity and metallic character, so one explanation carries several exam items.

Electron affinity is the energy released when an atom gains an electron, so a stronger pull releases more energy. Across a period the atom shrinks and the pull grows, so electron affinity rises; down a group new shells shield the nucleus, so it falls; chlorine is the classic exception, with the most exothermic electron affinity of any element. This is the same charge-versus-shielding contest, not a separate memorised list.
bullets: Across a period, charge wins and ionisation energy rises.
Down a group, shielding wins and ionisation energy falls.
Noble gases mark the peaks of the saw-tooth trend.
Reasons earn marks; recitation earns part marks.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why atomic radius falls across but rises down
paragraphs: Atomic radius is the distance from nucleus to outer electron. Across a period, protons increase while the shell stays the same, so the pull per electron grows and the atom shrinks. Sodium is larger than chlorine for this reason alone.

Down a group, a new shell is added each step, so even though protons increase, the outer electrons sit a whole layer farther out. Fluorine is therefore much smaller than bromine, despite having fewer protons.

Ionic radius follows the same contest with a twist: Na{{sup:+}} is smaller than the Na atom because it lost a shell, while Cl{{sup:-}} is larger than Cl because it gained one. Charge changes the shell count itself.
That twist is why radius questions often ask about ions rather than atoms. Convert the charge into a shell change before you compare, and you will never be trapped.
Radius values quoted for ions come from crystal measurements, and they follow the shell logic exactly: fewer shells, smaller ion; more shells, larger ion.
bullets: Across a period, atoms shrink as protons are added.
Down a group, atoms grow as shells are added.
Na{{sup:+}} shrank a shell; Cl{{sup:-}} gained one.
Convert the charge to a shell change first.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in the periodic table
paragraphs: The classic trap reverses the two directions: you recall that electronegativity rises across the period and then apply that rise down the group, where it actually falls. Before answering, name the direction, across or down, and only then pick the rising or falling trend.

The second trap is metallic character. It fades across the period (left is metallic, right is non-metallic) and grows down the group (heavier members are more metallic). Both statements are true; confusing which direction the question asks about is the error.

The third trap is position versus mechanism. Stating that Group 1 elements ‘are reactive’ earns nothing if you cannot explain that each has one outer electron to lose. The charge-versus-shielding mechanism is what earns the full mark.
The fourth trap is reading ‘increase’ as ‘decrease’ on a downward question. Writing the two arrows (across ↑, down ↓) beside every trend question removes this error almost entirely.
bullets: Name the direction before choosing the trend.
Metallic character fades across, grows down.
Reasons (charge vs shielding) earn the full mark.
Write the arrows beside every trend item.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonding
lessons.objective: Distinguish electrovalent (ionic), covalent, coordinate, hydrogen, metallic bonds and van der Waals forces, deduce bond types from electron configurations, relate bonding to properties of compounds, and differentiate the shapes of simple molecules (linear, non-linear, tetrahedral, pyramidal).

content.heading: Chemical Bonding
paragraphs: If bonding ever felt like a maze of names, here is the whole trick. Atoms do only two things with electrons: share or give. Every bond in this lesson, and every property that follows, comes down to that one choice.

content.heading: Giving and sharing electrons
paragraphs: Electrovalent (ionic) bonding is giving: a metal loses electrons and a non-metal gains them, so both become ions that attract each other. Sodium (2,8,1) gives one electron and chlorine (2,8,7) gains one, forming NaCl. The result is a lattice, like a criss-cross of opposite charges.

Covalent bonding is sharing: non-metals share electrons so each reaches a full outer shell. Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons to form H{{sub:2}}, and oxygen shares two pairs to form O{{sub:2}}. Water (H{{sub:2O}}) and methane (CH{{sub:4}}) are covalent because all their atoms are non-metals.

Ionic compounds melt high and conduct when molten or dissolved, because their ions are free to move. Covalent compounds usually melt low and never conduct, because they have no ions to move. Properties therefore announce the bonding.
bullets: Ionic = giving electrons (metal + non-metal).
Covalent = sharing electrons (non-metal + non-metal).
Ionic: high melting, conducts molten. Covalent: low melting, no conduction.
Properties announce the bonding.
content.takeaway: Giving makes ions and crystals; sharing makes molecules; properties tell which.

check.question: Magnesium (2,8,2) and chlorine (2,8,7) react. Which bonding results, and how many of each ion form?
options: Ionic bonding, one Mg{{sup:2+}} and two Cl{{sup:-}}
Ionic bonding, one Mg{{sup:+}} and one Cl{{sup:-}}
check.why: Magnesium loses two electrons to become Mg{{sup:2+}}, and two chlorines each gain one to become Cl{{sup:-}}.

content.heading: The special bonds
paragraphs: Metallic bonding is giving without keeping: metal atoms drop their outer electrons into a shared sea, and that sea holds the positive cores together. The shared sea is why metals conduct electricity and bend instead of breaking.

Hydrogen bonding is an attraction between molecules, which is why water boils so high. A coordinate (dative) bond is sharing where both electrons come from one atom, as in [Fe(CN){{sub:6}}]{{sup:4-}} (ferrocyanide), [Fe(CN){{sub:6}}]{{sup:3-}} and [Cu(NH{{sub:3}}){{sub:4}}]{{sup:2+}}.

Van der Waals forces are the weakest attractions between molecules, like the faint stickiness of loose pages. They matter only when stronger bonds are absent, which is why they are listed as a special weak force.
bullets: Metallic = shared electron sea; explains conductivity and malleability.
Hydrogen bond = extra attraction between molecules (water, HF, NH{{sub:3}}).
Coordinate bond = sharing where one atom supplies both electrons: [Fe(CN){{sub:6}}]{{sup:4-}}.
Van der Waals = weakest force between molecules.
content.takeaway: Metallic seas, hydrogen attractions and dative sharing are the special cases.

check.question: In [Cu(NH{{sub:3}}){{sub:4}}]{{sup:2+}}, where do the bonding electron pairs come from?
options: One comes from Cu and one from NH{{sub:3}}
Both come from the NH{{sub:3}} molecules
Both come from the copper ion
They are free electrons shared by the sea
check.why: In a coordinate bond one atom supplies both electrons: here NH{{sub:3}} supplies each pair.

content.heading: Shapes of molecules
paragraphs: The shape of a molecule depends on how its atoms arrange around the centre. A linear molecule is a straight line, like CO{{sub:2}}, HCl, H{{sub:2}}, O{{sub:2}} and Cl{{sub:2}}. A bent (non-linear) molecule folds at the centre, like H{{sub:2O}}, which is why its shape is described as V-shaped.

A tetrahedral molecule spreads four atoms to the corners of a pyramid, like CH{{sub:4}}. A trigonal pyramidal molecule spreads three atoms with a lone pair at the apex, like NH{{sub:3}}. The lone pair pushes the three atoms down, giving the pyramid its shape.

Shape predicts properties: bent water is polar while linear CO{{sub:2}} is not, and tetrahedral methane is symmetrical and non-polar. Picture the shape and you can predict polarity without memorising it.
bullets: Linear: CO{{sub:2}}, HCl, H{{sub:2}}, O{{sub:2}}, Cl{{sub:2}} (straight line).
Bent: H{{sub:2O}} (folds at oxygen).
Tetrahedral: CH{{sub:4}} (four corners). Pyramidal: NH{{sub:3}} (apex up).
Shape predicts polarity.
content.takeaway: Count the arrangement around the centre and the shape names itself.

check.question: Which molecule has a tetrahedral shape?
check.why: Methane spreads its four hydrogen atoms to the corners of a tetrahedron.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Decide the bonding from the electron counts first: a metal losing electrons means ionic, two non-metals sharing means covalent. The count decides before the name does.

content.problem: Deduce the bonding in MgCl{{sub:2}} from the electron counts Mg (2,8,2) and Cl (2,8,7).

steps.reason: Mg has 2 outer electrons; Cl needs 1. Best move: draw the electron-dot sharing between them. If the configurations are not printed, use the electronegativity difference instead.
steps.predictPrompt: What information do you compare before deciding?

steps.reason: A metal always gives; its 2 electrons go to two chlorines.
steps.predictPrompt: What exactly does the question want you to write down first?

steps.reason: One Mg{{sup:2+}} balances two Cl{{sup:-}}, and ionic solids melt high.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

steps.reason: Cl{{sub:2}} bonds covalently; two chlorines share rather than give.
steps.result: Metal + non-metal = ionic; non-metal + non-metal = covalent
steps.predictPrompt: What happens when both atoms refuse to give?

steps.operation: Check to confirm: balance the charges
steps.reason: One Mg{{sup:2+}} and two Cl{{sup:-}} must total zero; a wrong count breaks the neutral formula.
steps.result: (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0, so MgCl{{sub:2}} is neutral as written
steps.predictPrompt: Do the charges add to zero in MgCl{{sub:2}}?

content.problem: Predict and explain the shape and polarity of CO₂, given that carbon has 4 outer electrons and oxygen has 6.

steps.reason: each oxygen shares 2 with carbon; carbon shares its own 4 two-at-a-time
steps.result: two C=O double bonds, no lone pairs on carbon
steps.predictPrompt: Why double bonds rather than single?

steps.reason: the two double bonds repel each other and arrange 180° apart
steps.predictPrompt: Why do the two repelling regions pull to opposite ends?

steps.reason: each C=O bond is polar, but the two bond dipoles are equal and cancel across the linear axis
steps.predictPrompt: Why do the two identical dipoles cancel instead of adding?

steps.operation: Check to confirm: compare the sibling bent water molecule
steps.reason: water bent at ~105° does not cancel its dipoles — CO₂ does because both ends are identical
steps.result: asymmetry decides polarity, not bond count
steps.predictPrompt: What makes the one cancel and the other not?

content.question: Sodium (2,8,1) reacts with chlorine (2,8,7). Deduce the bonding, the ions formed and the formula.
hints: Sodium is a metal: what does it do with its one electron?
Chlorine needs one electron, so one sodium feeds one chlorine
Write the ions, then drop the charges into the formula

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved
paragraphs: In solid NaCl, the ions are locked in a rigid lattice and cannot move, so no current flows even though charges are present. Melting or dissolving frees the ions to drift to the electrodes, and conduction begins. Conductivity is therefore about the freedom of ions, not the mere presence of charge.

Covalent compounds never conduct, even molten, because they contain no ions at all, only neutral molecules. Diamond and graphite differ here because graphite has free electrons between its layers, a rare covalent exception.

You can be tested on the prediction, not the definition: given a new compound's melting point and conductivity, name its bonding. High melting plus conduction when molten means ionic; low melting with no conduction means covalent.
That prediction skill is exactly what JAMB questions measure. Bonding names, shapes and properties are one chain, and the chain starts at the electron count.
The same logic runs backwards: when a solution is evaporated, the ions lock back into a lattice and conduction stops. Freedom of ions is switched on and off by state, not by composition.
JAMB items exploit this directly, asking why solid NaCl fails to conduct while its melt succeeds. The answer is always the locked ions, never the absence of charge.
bullets: Solid ionic: ions locked, no conduction.
Molten or dissolved: ions free, conduction starts.
Covalent: no ions at all, so no conduction ever.
Predict bonding from melting point and conductivity.

content.heading: Go deeper: Hydrogen bonding versus ordinary dipole forces
paragraphs: Ordinary dipole attraction happens between any polar molecules: the positive end of one is faintly attracted to the negative end of another. Hydrogen bonding is a stronger, special case that needs a hydrogen atom bonded directly to N, O or F.

That is why water (H{{sub:2O}}) boils at 100 °C while methane (CH{{sub:4}}), of similar size, boils far lower. Each water molecule hydrogen-bonds to its neighbours, and much heat is needed to break those links. HF and NH{{sub:3}} show the same elevation.

Van der Waals forces are weaker still and act between all molecules, polar or not. They become noticeable only when hydrogen bonding is absent, which is why small non-polar molecules are gases at room temperature.

The exam ordering (hydrogen bond strongest, then dipole, then van der Waals weakest) is therefore a ranking of separation distances. Stronger attraction means a higher boiling point, and the ranking sorts every comparison question.
bullets: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.
Water boils high because of hydrogen bonding.
Dipole forces are weaker; van der Waals weakest.
Stronger attraction means higher boiling point.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in bonding
paragraphs: The classic trap swaps giving and sharing: calling NaCl covalent because ‘atoms are joined’. The test is the participants: a metal plus a non-metal always gives, so the bond is ionic. Name the participants first, then the bond.

The second trap is calling any attraction a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to N, O or F; the attraction in HCl is a dipole force, not a hydrogen bond. The bonded atom matters, not the presence of hydrogen alone.

The third trap is the shape swap between NH{{sub:3}} (pyramidal) and CH{{sub:4}} (tetrahedral). Counting the atoms is not enough; NH{{sub:3}} has a lone pair pushing down, which makes it a pyramid with an apex, not a tetrahedron.

The fourth trap is the coordinate bond. It looks like ordinary sharing, but one atom supplies both electrons. In [Ag(NH{{sub:3}}){{sub:2}}]{{sup:+}} the silver ion accepts pairs from ammonia; the donor is always the ligand, never the metal.
A final trap is calling metal atoms ‘molecules’. Metals are lattices of atoms, not discrete molecules, which is why metals melt as a whole rather than boiling into single atoms.
bullets: Metal + non-metal = ionic, always.
Hydrogen bond needs H on N, O or F.
NH{{sub:3}} is pyramidal (lone pair); CH{{sub:4}} is tetrahedral.
In coordinate bonds the ligand donates both electrons.

lessons.title: Separation of Mixtures
lessons.objective: Distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures, differentiate chemical from physical changes, distinguish pure from impure substances, use melting/boiling points as purity criteria, and specify the principle and everyday use of each separation method (evaporation, distillation, sublimation, re-crystallisation, chromatography, crystallisation, magnetisation, decantation, filtration, centrifugation).

content.heading: Separation of Mixtures
paragraphs: Separation can feel like a long list of laboratory tricks, but every single method boils down to one idea: pick the parts apart by the one difference between them. This lesson walks through those differences so you can spot the right tool for any mixture.

content.heading: Elements, compounds and mixtures
paragraphs: An element is one kind of atom, like oxygen. A compound is elements joined by chemical bonding, like water. A mixture is substances merely mixed, like sand and salt.
A chemical change makes a new substance with new properties, like burning wood. A physical change changes only appearance, like melting ice. Mixtures change physically, so their parts separate again.

A pure substance melts and boils sharply at one temperature; an impure one melts over a range. A falling melting point therefore reveals impurities, which makes melting and boiling points purity tests.

Density and freezing point also test purity: a pure substance has a fixed density and a sharp freezing point. Impurities shift density and depress or spread the freezing point, so an off-value proves impurity.
bullets: Element = one atom kind; compound = bonded; mixture = mixed.
Chemical change makes new substances; physical change does not.
Pure melts sharply; impure melts over a range.
Pure: fixed density and sharp freezing point; impure: shifted, spread values.
content.takeaway: Mixtures separate physically because their parts were never bonded.

check.question: Which statement correctly pairs a pure substance with its test?
options: A pure substance melts at one exact temperature
Impure substances boil at one exact temperature
check.why: Purity shows as a sharp melting point; impurities spread the range.

content.heading: Separating by heat and air
paragraphs: Evaporation removes a liquid by heating, leaving the dissolved solid: salt from seawater is won this way. Simple distillation separates liquids with different boiling points, like ethanol and water, by boiling and condensing the vapour. Fractional distillation repeats that for many fractions, as in crude oil refining.

Sublimation turns a solid directly into vapour, as with camphor or ammonium chloride, which then deposits back. Re-crystallisation dissolves the solid hot and cools the solution so pure crystals form. Each method exploits one property: volatility, boiling point or solubility.

Magnetisation removes iron with a magnet, as in scrapyards. Decantation pours the liquid off a solid, filtration traps the solid, and centrifugation spins a mixture so the denser part settles outward, as in blood tests.
bullets: Evaporation leaves the salt; distillation separates by boiling point.
Sublimation: solid → vapour → solid (camphor, NH{{sub:4Cl}}).
Magnet removes iron; decantation pours; filtration traps; centrifugation spins.
Every method exploits one property difference.
content.takeaway: Find the property that differs, and that property is the separating tool.

visual.caption: Each method works because one property differs, and that difference is the separating tool.

check.question: To obtain pure water from seawater that also contains suspended sand, which order of methods works?
check.why: Filtration removes sand first, then distillation separates water from dissolved salt.

content.heading: Chromatography and crystallisation
paragraphs: Chromatography separates dyes travelling at different speeds along a strip. Paper chromatography dips ink in water; the colours spread as bands. Column chromatography holds back some parts longer in a packed tube.

Simple crystallisation grows crystals from a saturated solution by cooling or evaporation. Re-crystallisation purifies: dissolve the impure solid hot, filter while hot, then cool so only pure crystals form while impurities stay dissolved.
The underlying principle is solubility: parts dissolve or travel at different rates. The differing property chooses the method.

Fractional crystallisation separates two soluble salts with close solubilities, like saltpetre and common salt, crystallising one then the other as the solution cools. Simple crystallisation grows one salt at a time; fractional separates a pair by staged cooling.
bullets: Paper chromatography separates ink dyes by travel speed.
Column chromatography holds components back differently.
Crystallisation uses solubility; re-crystallisation purifies.
Fractional separates close pairs in stages; simple grows one salt.
content.takeaway: Chromatography separates by speed; crystallisation separates by solubility.

check.question: Black ink is mainly one dye that travels as a single band. What does that tell you about its composition?
options: It contains several dyes travelling together
check.why: A single band means the ink is essentially one dye; several dyes would spread into several bands.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before you name a method, name the property that differs: boiling point, solubility, density or magnetism. The property chooses the method every time.

content.problem: A mixture holds sand, salt and water. Describe a separation that gives pure water.

steps.reason: Sand is insoluble; the filter traps it and the salt water passes. Best move: filter, then distil for pure water. If only salt is wanted, just evaporate to dryness.
steps.result: Sand is removed as a solid
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.reason: Water boils and condenses; salt does not distil.
steps.result: Pure water is collected, salt remains in the flask
steps.predictPrompt: What exactly does the question want you to write down first?

steps.reason: Evaporating to dryness would leave salt with nothing pure to collect.
steps.result: Distillation is needed to collect the water itself

steps.reason: Oil floats on water instead of dissolving.

content.problem: A mixture of two dyes is chromatographed on paper. After 20 minutes the solvent front is at 5.0 cm from the baseline. One dye has travelled 4.5 cm, the other 3.0 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value of the faster dye.

steps.reason: Rf = distance travelled by the spot / distance travelled by the solvent front
steps.predictPrompt: Why divide by the solvent front and not 100?
Is this plausible between 0 and 1?

steps.reason: an Rf of 0.9 means this dye travels nearly as fast as the solvent front under these conditions
steps.result: the faster dye has Rf 0.9; the slower has Rf 3.0 / 5.0 = 0.6
