steps.operation: Check to confirm: the other dye
steps.reason: Rf(slower) = 3.0 / 5.0 = 0.6 — ratio of 4.5 to 3.0 equals Rf ratio 0.9 to 0.6 = 3/2
steps.result: both dyes measured from the same front give consistent results
steps.predictPrompt: Do the two Rf values confirm the same solvent conditions?

content.question: A mixture holds iron filings, sand and water. Give a two-step separation that recovers the iron and the water.
hints: One component answers to a magnet
After that, separate the solid from the water by filtering
Then distil to collect the water pure

content.heading: Go deeper: Why fractional distillation beats simple
paragraphs: Simple distillation separates two liquids with widely different boiling points. Crude oil holds many fractions with boiling points close together, so one round of boiling cannot divide them. Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column where vapours rise, cool and condense at their own levels.

Each level of the column is a separate still in miniature: vapour condenses, re-boils and rises again. The lightest fraction escapes at the top, while heavier ones leave lower down. The column therefore multiplies the separation without multiplying the apparatus.
The same principle refines air into oxygen and nitrogen, and petroleum into petrol, kerosene and diesel. Whenever boiling points crowd together, fractionation is the answer.
Once you link the column to repeated simple distillations, you will never mistake a single flask for a fractionating column again.

A simple still can split two liquids when their boiling points differ by a wide margin, because the lower-boiling vapour leaves alone. As the gap narrows, contamination rises, and only the column's repeated boil–condense cycles keep the fractions apart.
bullets: Crude oil fractions boil too close for one still.
The column repeats boil–condense at each level.
Light fractions exit top; heavy fractions exit lower.
Fractionation is repeated simple distillation in one tower.

content.heading: Go deeper: Chromatography as identity evidence
paragraphs: The retention factor, Rf, measures how far a spot travelled relative to the solvent: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent. A spot that always travels to the same Rf is the same substance in different hands, which makes chromatography an identity test, not only a separation tool.

Two dyes with different Rf values separate into different bands, and the pattern of bands is a fingerprint. Food colours, inks and plant pigments are all identified this way in food and forensic laboratories.

Paper chromatography depends on solubility and attraction to paper; column chromatography adds adsorption on the packing. Both exploit the same difference: how strongly each component holds on versus travels on.
The exam trap is to treat Rf as a separation product. Rf identifies; it does not manufacture. The discovery of a new spot means a new dye, not a new element.

Because each substance has a fixed Rf under given conditions, matching Rf values in two samples is strong evidence that they contain the same dye. Courts and food laboratories rely on exactly this reasoning.
The solvent must be chosen so the spots travel a measurable distance without running off the paper. A solvent in which the dye is insoluble gives no evidence at all.
bullets: Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance.
Rf patterns identify dyes and pigments.
Paper uses solubility; column adds adsorption.
Rf identifies; it does not create new substances.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in separation
paragraphs: The first trap is melting-point reading. A substance melting over a range is impure, but a substance melting sharply is not necessarily pure; some mixtures melt sharply by coincidence. Sharpness is evidence, not proof, and it is worth stating it that way in an answer.

The second trap confuses sublimation with evaporation. Evaporation turns a liquid into vapour; sublimation turns a solid directly into vapour. Camphor and ammonium chloride sublime; water evaporates. The starting state decides the name.

The third trap mixes decantation with filtration. Decantation pours the liquid off; filtration passes the mixture through a barrier. If the solid is fine enough to pass the filter, decantation fails and centrifugation is the answer.

The fourth trap is choosing distillation for immiscible liquids. Oil and water separate by decantation long before boiling is needed; distillation is the tool when boiling points differ, not whenever two liquids mix.

A final trap is over-heating during evaporation to dryness, which decomposes some salts. Gentle heating and crystallisation on cooling are the safe route, and the question usually hints at it by asking for crystals.
bullets: Sharp melting is evidence, not proof, of purity.
Sublimation starts from a solid; evaporation from a liquid.
Decantation pours; filtration traps; centrifugation spins.
Immiscible liquids separate without boiling.

lessons.title: Solubility
lessons.objective: Distinguish unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions, interpret solubility curves, calculate the amount of solute that dissolves at a given temperature, relate solvents to their uses, and differentiate true solutions from suspensions and colloids with examples.

content.heading: Solubility
paragraphs: Solubility decides whether tea dissolves your sugar, whether ink stains your clothes and whether a river survives summer. It is one idea, how much a given amount of liquid can dissolve, and this lesson gives you the limit, the calculation and the exceptions.

content.heading: Full, not full, and over-full
paragraphs: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more, like a half-filled cup. A saturated solution is full: at that temperature it can dissolve no more, and any extra solid settles. A supersaturated solution is over-full; it holds more than the limit because it was cooled carefully without anything to start crystallisation.

A solubility curve shows how much dissolves at each temperature. Most salts dissolve more as water warms, so their curve climbs. Gases behave oppositely: oxygen dissolves less in warm water, which is why warm water holds less dissolved air for fish.

Solubility is written in mol/dm{{sup:3}}: moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution. At saturation, the concentration is fixed by the temperature, not by how much solid you added; extra solid just sits at the bottom.
bullets: Unsaturated: more can dissolve. Saturated: full. Supersaturated: over-full.
Most salts dissolve more when hot; gases dissolve less when hot.
Solubility = moles of solute per dm{{sup:3}} of saturated solution.
content.takeaway: Solubility is a limit set by temperature, and the curve shows how it moves.

check.question: A solution holds more solute than the maximum at that temperature. What is it?
check.why: Holding more than the maximum means the solution is supersaturated.

visual.caption: Heating dissolves more until full, and careful cooling can push past full into over-full.

content.heading: Calculating solubility and choosing solvents
paragraphs: A solubility calculation starts from the definition: how many moles sit in one dm{{sup:3}} of saturated solution. Suppose 11 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.1 dm{{sup:3}}. Moles = 11 ÷ 58.5 = 0.188 mol, so the solubility is 0.188 ÷ 0.1 = 1.88 mol/dm{{sup:3}}.

Like dissolves like: water, a polar liquid, removes sweat and salt, but not grease. Petrol, an organic solvent, dissolves grease and paint, which is why dry cleaners use it. Fats need detergent; oil needs turpentine; the solvent must match the stain.
Temperature enters every calculation. A curve reading gives solubility at that temperature, and a supersaturated solution made hot may crash out crystals on cooling, the basis of re-crystallisation.
bullets: Molar solubility = moles ÷ volume of saturated solution.
Water removes polar stains; petrol removes grease and paint.
The solvent is matched to the nature of the stain.
Oil needs turpentine/organic solvents; fats need detergents.
content.takeaway: Solubility is moles per dm{{sup:3}} at saturation, and the solvent must match the stain.

check.question: Which solvent best removes engine grease from cloth?
check.why: Grease is non-polar like petrol, so petrol dissolves it while water does not.

content.heading: True solutions, suspensions and colloids
paragraphs: A true solution is uniform at the particle level: sugar in water looks clear, passes through filter paper, and never settles. A suspension has particles large enough to see and settle, like muddy water after stirring.

A colloid sits between the two: its particles are too small to see or filter but large enough to scatter light. Fog, milk, blood, aerosol sprays, emulsion paints, Harmattan haze (dust in air) and rubber solution are colloids. The Tyndall effect, a light beam turning visible, is the giveaway.
Particle size decides everything: true solutions pass filter paper; colloids scatter light but do not settle; suspensions settle and are filtered. Size, not appearance, is the distinction.
bullets: True solution: uniform, passes filters, never settles.
Suspension: visible particles, settles, filtered (haze, water paints).
Colloid: invisible particles, scatters light (fog, milk, blood).
Particle size separates the three.
content.takeaway: Size decides: solutions pass, colloids scatter, suspensions settle.

check.question: Which mixture is a colloid?
check.why: Fog scatters light and resists filtration like other colloids, unlike the suspensions and true solution.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any solubility number, ask which temperature it belongs to. A solubility quoted without its temperature means nothing, and examiners plant exactly that trap.

content.problem: 11 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.1 dm{{sup:3}} of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.

steps.reason: Moles = mass ÷ Mr. Best move: this formula works on any masses you hold. If only grammes per 100 cm{{sup:3}} are printed, work the ratio straight out.
steps.predictPrompt: Which numbers or terms work with each other first?

steps.reason: Solubility is measured per cubic decimetre of solution.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you verify this answer?

steps.reason: 0.188 × 58.5 = 11.0, so the division is exact.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

steps.reason: Double the water (0.2 dm{{sup:3}}) halves c to 0.94 mol/dm{{sup:3}}.
steps.result: c halves when the same solute gets double the solvent
steps.predictPrompt: What happens if the volume were doubled?

steps.operation: Check to confirm: rebuild the 11 g
steps.reason: Concentration × volume × Mr must hand back the dissolved mass; a mismatch means the division slipped.
steps.predictPrompt: Can you rebuild 11 g from 1.88 mol/dm{{sup:3}}?

content.problem: 40 g of potassium nitrate dissolves in 0.2 dm3 of solution. Find its molar solubility. (Ar K=39, N=14, O=16)

steps.predictPrompt: Why 3 x 16 and not 16 alone?

steps.reason: moles = mass / Mr = 40 / 101
steps.predictPrompt: Estimate: under 0.4, yes?

steps.reason: one mole dissolves per 101 g — divide by volume
steps.predictPrompt: Is this more or less than 2 M?
Do you land on the original 40 g?

content.question: 23.4 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.2 dm{{sup:3}} of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why gases dissolve less when hot
paragraphs: Dissolving a gas means trapping its particles into the liquid. Warming speeds particles up, so they escape more easily, the same reason a hot drink goes flat. Salts behave oppositely because warming helps break their lattice apart.

That opposite behaviour is why solubility curves split into two families: climbing curves for salts, falling curves for gases. Sodium sulphate decahydrate is the exception that proves the rule, falling after about 33 °C when it loses its water of crystallisation.

The practical effect is everywhere: soft drinks are bottled cold to keep gas in, and heating water drives dissolved air out as bubbles. Temperature dependence is not a formula detail; it is visible in every cold drink.
Once you can explain the escape idea, you can predict the direction of any curve without memorising it. Hot liquid cannot hold fast-moving gas particles.
The same escape logic explains why a heated soft drink releases bubbles immediately. The gas was only ever loosely held, and warming loosens its grip further.
At the other end, cooling a gas makes it far more soluble, which is why winter lakes hold more dissolved oxygen for fish.
bullets: Gas solubility falls with temperature (particles escape).
Most salts rise; gases fall: two curve families.
Cold drinks stay fizzy because cold holds gas.
One escape picture predicts every direction.

content.heading: Go deeper: Supersaturation and how it forms
paragraphs: A supersaturated solution holds more solute than its temperature allows, but only because crystallisation has not started. Stirring, scratching or adding a tiny crystal starts the process, and the excess falls out until saturation returns.

It is made by dissolving at a high temperature, filtering while hot to remove impurities, then cooling slowly without disturbance. Rock candy is grown exactly this way: a supersaturated sugar solution cooling around a string.
Supersaturation is unstable by definition; the excess wants out. That instability is useful for purification: the excess crashes out as pure crystals while impurities stay dissolved.

The exam trap is calling a supersaturated solution ‘concentrated’. Concentration is a measurement; supersaturation is a state beyond the saturation limit. A solution can be concentrated without being supersaturated.
A careful chemist can recrystallise a salt that refuses to dissolve cold: dissolve it hot, remove impurities by hot filtration, then seed the cooling solution with a pure crystal.
Without the seed, a supersaturated solution can sit stable for days, a reminder that stability in chemistry is often only the absence of a beginning.
bullets: Supersaturated = more than the limit, waiting for a start.
Made by hot dissolving, hot filtering, slow cooling.
Used to purify salts by re-crystallisation.
Concentrated is a measure; supersaturated is a state.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in solubility
paragraphs: The first trap confuses solubility with concentration. Solubility is the saturation limit at a temperature; concentration is what is actually present. A dilute solution may be far below its solubility, and a supersaturated one far above.

The second trap mixes gramme solubility with molar solubility. Converting between them needs Mr: grammes per dm{{sup:3}} divided by Mr gives mol/dm{{sup:3}}. Skipping Mr is the commonest calculation error in this topic.
The third trap ignores the curve's temperature. Reading a value from the wrong temperature point is reading a different solution entirely. Always anchor the reading to the stated temperature.
The fourth trap treats colloids as suspensions. Both look milky, but colloids do not settle and pass neither filter nor light beam silently. Particle size, not appearance, decides the class.
A final trap is treating the Tyndall effect as proof of a true solution. Only colloids scatter a beam of light; a clear true solution leaves the beam invisible.

Curve-based mass questions follow the same anchor rule: read the solubility value at the stated temperature, then scale it to the given solvent mass. If a curve gives 40 g per 100 g water at 30 °C, then 200 g water dissolves 80 g at that temperature. The reading decides everything; the arithmetic is just a ratio.
bullets: Solubility is the limit; concentration is the present amount.
Convert g/dm{{sup:3}} to mol/dm{{sup:3}} by dividing by Mr.
Anchor every curve reading to its temperature.
Colloids scatter light; suspensions settle.

lessons.title: Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)
lessons.objective: Classify reactions in terms of oxidation and reduction in their three senses (oxygen, hydrogen/electron transfer, oxidation number), deduce oxidation numbers, balance simple redox equations, compute electrons transferred, name species and agents, and apply oxidation numbers in naming inorganic compounds.

content.heading: Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)
paragraphs: A cut apple browns in the air, and an iron nail loses its shine to rust. Both are the same kind of change: gaining oxygen or losing electrons. Redox sounds intimidating because the names are old, but the idea is one you already know. This lesson gives you three ways to spot it and one number that tracks it.

content.heading: Three ways to spot the change
paragraphs: In the oxygen sense, oxidation means gaining oxygen: copper heated in air becomes black copper(II) oxide. Reduction is the reverse, removing oxygen, often with hydrogen: hydrogen strips oxygen from copper(II) oxide and leaves copper metal. The brown apple gained oxygen; the nail does the same.

In the electron sense, oxidation means losing electrons and reduction means gaining them. Sodium becomes Na{{sup:+}} by losing one electron, so sodium is oxidised; chlorine becomes Cl{{sup:-}} by gaining one, so chlorine is reduced. The memory aid OIL RIG says: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain, of electrons.
In the oxidation-number sense, oxidation is an increase in oxidation number and reduction is a decrease. All three senses describe the same event; they are three languages for one change.
bullets: Oxygen sense: oxidation = gains O; reduction = loses O.
Electron sense: oxidation = loses e{{sup:-}}; reduction = gains e{{sup:-}}.
OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.
Number sense: rise = oxidation, fall = reduction.
content.takeaway: Oxidation and reduction are gain and loss: of oxygen, then of electrons.

check.question: In the reaction 2Cu + O{{sub:2}} → 2CuO, copper is
options: unchanged because oxygen is a spectator
check.why: Copper gains oxygen, and also loses electrons, so it is oxidised.

content.heading: Oxidation numbers as bookkeeping
paragraphs: An oxidation number is a piece of bookkeeping: free elements score zero; monatomic ions equal their charges; H is +1, O is −2; the sum is zero in a neutral compound.
The change in oxidation number counts electrons moved. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, a fall of 5, so each permanganate gains 5 electrons. That count is what balancing uses.
bullets: Free element = 0; monatomic ion = its charge.
H is +1; O is −2; sums to zero in compounds.
Mn in KMnO{{sub:4}} is +7; S in H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}} is +6; Cr in Cr{{sub:2O}}{{sub:7}}{{sup:2-}} is +6.
A fall of 5 in oxidation number means 5 electrons gained.
content.takeaway: Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping: the change counts the electrons.

check.question: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}}?
check.why: 2 + S − 8 = 0 gives S = +6.

content.heading: Balancing, naming and testing
paragraphs: Half-equations balance atoms and charge together. In MnO{{sub:4}}{{sup:-}} + 5Fe{{sup:2+}} + 8H{{sup:+}} → Mn{{sup:2+}} + 5Fe{{sup:3+}} + 4H{{sub:2O}}, manganese falls 5 (from +7 to +2) and iron rises 1 each, so 5 irons match one permanganate. Balancing by oxidation number is counting the fall against the rise.
Oxidation numbers name compounds: iron(II) chloride has Fe at +2, iron(III) chloride at +3. The Roman numeral is the oxidation number in words, which is why the same metal gives two different names.

Oxidising agents take electrons: acidified dichromate turns green when reduced. Reducing agents give electrons: hydrogen bleaches hot copper(II) oxide. The agent is named by what it does to the other reactant, not by what happens to itself.
bullets: Balance by matching the oxidation-number change.
Iron(II) = +2; iron(III) = +3; the numeral names the state.
Oxidising agent takes electrons; reducing agent gives them.
Acidified dichromate turns green when reduced.
content.takeaway: Count the fall against the rise and the equation balances itself.

check.question: In MnO{{sub:4}}{{sup:-}} + 5Fe{{sup:2+}} + 8H{{sup:+}} → Mn{{sup:2+}} + 5Fe{{sup:3+}} + 4H{{sub:2O}}, which species is the oxidising agent?
check.why: MnO{{sub:4}}{{sup:-}} is reduced from +7 to +2, so it oxidises Fe{{sup:2+}}.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When you balance, write the oxidation-number change under each changing atom first. The matching fall and rise tell you the coefficients before you count charge.

content.problem: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H{{sub:2S}}{{sub:2O}}{{sub:3}} (thiosulphuric acid)?

steps.reason: H is +1, O is −2; these rarely budge. Best move: assign those first. If the molecule is neutral, make every oxidation number add up to zero.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: A neutral compound sums to zero.
steps.predictPrompt: What do you need to find before you can solve this?

steps.reason: The two sulphurs share the +4 needed.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

steps.reason: Sulphur's highest common state is +6 (as in SO{{sub:4}}{{sup:2-}}).
steps.result: Any state above +6 means the sum rule was misapplied
steps.predictPrompt: What is sulphur's highest common oxidation state?

steps.operation: Check to confirm: substitute back into the sum
steps.reason: H{{sub:2S}}{{sub:2O}}{{sub:3}} is neutral, so the numbers must total zero; a wrong S value breaks the sum.
steps.predictPrompt: Does your S value make the whole molecule neutral?

content.problem: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Cr{{sub:2}}O{{sub:7}}{{sup:2-}}?

steps.operation: Set the sum equal to the charge
steps.reason: sum = -2 because of the {{sub:7}} charge on the ion
steps.predictPrompt: Why -2 and not +2?
Does this line snap back?

steps.reason: chromium sits at +6 in dichromate
steps.predictPrompt: Is this the famous orange colour level?

steps.operation: Check to confirm: sum the whole ion
steps.reason: 2(+6) + 7(-2) = 12 - 14 = -2 exactly equal the ion charge
steps.predictPrompt: Do the parts add to the whole?

content.question: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Cr{{sub:2O}}{{sub:7}}{{sup:2-}}?

content.heading: Go deeper: Why oxidation number is bookkeeping
paragraphs: Oxidation number is not a real charge on the atom; it is an accounting entry. In NaCl, sodium has truly lost its electron to chlorine, but in CO the numbers +2 and −2 are formal. The bookkeeping still predicts reactions because it tracks electron movement.
That is why peroxides surprise people: in H{{sub:2O}}{{sub:2}} each oxygen is −1, not −2, because they share. The exception only looks like one until you see the sharing.
Real charge and formal number agree only for ions. For molecules, the number is a tool for balancing, and the tool works precisely because it is consistent.
Treat the number as a real charge and you will misjudge covalent compounds. Treat it as bookkeeping and you can balance almost anything.
The bookkeeping is powerful because it is blind to real sharing: it assigns every electron to one atom by fixed rules, so reactions can be balanced without knowing the true electron distribution.
That blindness is also its limit. Oxidation numbers cannot say where electrons truly sit in a molecule, only how they are counted for equation purposes.
bullets: Oxidation number is formal, not a real charge.
Peroxides: O is −1 because of sharing.
The number tracks electron movement for balancing.
Bookkeeping mindset prevents errors in covalent compounds.

content.heading: Go deeper: Balancing half-equations step by step
paragraphs: The MnO{{sub:4}}{{sup:-}} + Fe{{sup:2+}} case shows the full method. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, a fall of 5, so each permanganate gains 5 electrons. Iron rises from +2 to +3, a rise of 1, so one iron gives 1 electron.

Balancing the fall against the rise needs 5 irons per permanganate; that fixes the 5 coefficient. Oxygen and hydrogen are then balanced with H{{sup:+}} and H{{sub:2O}}, and the charge is checked last.
The charge check is the safety net: left side −1 + 10 + 8 = +17; right side +2 + 15 = +17. Both sides match, so the equation is balanced. A mismatch means you missed an atom count somewhere.
The same ladder works for dichromate reductions and any half-equation the syllabus sets. Fall against rise, then atoms, then charge, in that order, every time.

In acid solution the needed H{{sup:+}} and H{{sub:2O}} are always available; in alkaline solution OH{{sup:-}} and H{{sub:2O}} play that role instead. The medium decides which species appears, and the question will name it.
Check the charge after every adjustment and you catch errors at the step where they appear, not at the end of the question.

Agent tests always name the colour that betrays the transfer. Acidified dichromate (orange) turns green as Cr{{sub:2O}}{{sub:7}}{{sup:2-}} is reduced to Cr{{sup:3+}}, while purple KMnO{{sub:4}} is bleached to colourless Mn{{sup:2+}} when it oxidises a reductant. Fe{{sup:2+}} (pale green) reduces dichromate and permanganate, whereas Fe{{sup:3+}} (brown) oxidises iodide to brown iodine.
bullets: Fall of 5 needs 5 irons rising by 1 each.
Balance O and H with water and H{{sup:+}}, check charge last.
Charge matching is the safety net.
Order: fall vs rise, atoms, charge.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in redox
paragraphs: The classic trap confuses oxidation with the oxidising agent. If copper is oxidised, copper is the reducing agent because it gave the electrons. Naming what a species does to the other reactant is the skill, and the trap reverses it.

The second trap is the sign of the change. A decrease in oxidation number is reduction, even though the atom ‘lost’ number; people read the smaller number as oxidation. Fall is reduction, rise is oxidation: the number moves opposite to the name.

The third trap is the oxygen rule with peroxides. In H{{sub:2O}}{{sub:2}} the oxygen is −1, and applying −2 gives a wrong sulphur count in thiosulphates. The shared oxygen is the exception that examiners plant.
The fourth trap is naming. Iron(II) chloride is not iron with two chlorides for fun; the numeral is the oxidation state itself, and swapping II and III swaps the formula.
A final trap is forgetting that an element in a free state is always zero, even nitrogen in N{{sub:2}} or oxygen in O{{sub:2}}. Assigning it a charge breaks every balance that follows.

The central atom oxidation state sets the suffix: the higher state takes -ate and the lower takes -ite, as in sulphate and sulphite. A variable metal takes a Roman numeral for its state, as in iron(II) and iron(III). The suffix and numeral both read the oxidation number directly.
bullets: Oxidised species is the reducing agent.
Fall in number = reduction; rise = oxidation.
Peroxide oxygen is −1, not −2.
The Roman numeral is the oxidation state.
Higher state takes -ate (sulphate); lower takes -ite (sulphite); metals take Roman numerals.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
lessons.objective: Distinguish the properties of acids and bases, determine basicity, classify normal, acidic, basic and double salts, state methods of preparing salts, relate conductance to degree of dissociation, perform pH and pOH calculations, state the significance of pH, apply buffer solutions, choose indicators, and balance the hydrolysis of salts.

content.heading: Acids, Bases and Salts
paragraphs: Every cook knows vinegar stains cloth and caustic soda dissolves blocked drains. They look similar, yet their chemistry is opposite. This lesson shows you how to tell them apart, what salts really are and why a titration flask decides so much.

content.heading: What acids and bases do
paragraphs: An acid is a substance whose water solution gives H{{sub:3O}}{{sup:+}} ions; it donates a proton. Acids turn blue litmus red, react with metals and carbonates, and form salts. A base is the opposite: it neutralises an acid, turning red litmus blue and forming a salt.

Basicity counts the hydrogen atoms an acid can donate: HCl is monobasic (one H), H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}} is dibasic (two H). Strong acids like HCl dissolve fully in water; weak acids like ethanoic acid (vinegar) dissolve only partly. Citric and tartaric acids are natural weak acids (oranges, tamarind).

Indicators show the difference without tasting: litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein change colour across the pH range. A buffer solution is a mixture that resists pH change, like the bicarbonate system that holds blood at pH 7.4.
bullets: Acids donate protons; bases accept them.
Strong acids dissociate fully; weak acids partly.
Indicators change colour across the pH range.
Buffers resist pH change.
content.takeaway: Acids donate protons, bases accept them and indicators show which is which.

check.question: Which definition of an acid follows the proton-donor idea?
options: A substance whose aqueous solution furnishes H{{sub:3O}}{{sup:+}} ions
A substance that turns red litmus blue
A substance that neutralises an acid
A substance that conducts electricity only when molten
check.why: Furnishing H{{sub:3O}}{{sup:+}} is exactly donating a proton to water.

content.heading: Salts and how they are made
paragraphs: A salt is the neutral product of an acid reacting with a base, metal or carbonate. If all the acid's replaceable hydrogen is replaced, the salt is normal: NaCl, NH{{sub:4Cl}}, Na{{sub:2CO}}{{sub:3}}. If some hydrogen remains replaceable, the salt is acidic: NaHSO{{sub:4}} is the classic example. If some hydroxide remains, the salt is basic: Mg(OH)Cl.

Double salts hold two salts together; alums are the classic case. Salts come from neutralisation, precipitation (two solutions forming an insoluble salt) or Zn + dilute H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}} → ZnSO{{sub:4}} + H{{sub:2}}.

How well a solution conducts depends on how far it dissociates. A strong acid dissociates fully and conducts well; a weak acid dissociates partly and conducts weakly. Conductance follows the ion count, not the concentration.
bullets: Normal salts use all replaceable H (NaCl, NH{{sub:4Cl}}); acidic salts keep some (NaHSO{{sub:4}}); basic salts keep OH (Mg(OH)Cl).
Alums are double salts.
Salts: neutralisation, precipitation, or acid on metal.
Conductance follows the ions present.
content.takeaway: Salt type names its leftover hydrogen or hydroxide; strength means dissociation.

check.question: NH{{sub:4Cl}} is an example of which salt type?
check.why: HCl is monobasic, every replaceable hydrogen is replaced in NH{{sub:4Cl}}, so NH{{sub:4Cl}} is a normal salt. Its solution is acidic because NH{{sub:4}}{{sup:+}} hydrolyses, not because of the salt type.

content.heading: pH, titration and hydrolysis
paragraphs: The pH scale counts hydrogen ions by their power of ten: pH = −log[H{{sup:+}}], so [H{{sup:+}}] = 1×10{{sup:-3}} mol/dm{{sup:3}} means pH 3. At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, so pOH = 14 − pH. Pure water sits at 7.

pH matters daily: the stomach works near pH 1–2, soil suits crops near 6–7 and blood holds 7.4. An indicator marks the titration end point: phenolphthalein for a strong acid with a strong base, methyl orange for a strong acid with a weak base.

Hydrolysis is a salt reacting with water, and it sets the solution's character. NH{{sub:4Cl}} hydrolyses acidic; Na{{sub:2CO}}{{sub:3}} hydrolyses basic. Their equations: NH{{sub:4}}{{sup:+}} + H{{sub:2O}} ⇌ NH{{sub:3}} + H{{sub:3O}}{{sup:+}} and CO{{sub:3}}{{sup:2-}} + H{{sub:2O}} ⇌ HCO{{sub:3}}{{sup:-}} + OH{{sup:-}}. The ion that hydrolyses decides the result.
bullets: pH = −log[H{{sup:+}}]; pOH = 14 − pH.
Blood 7.4; stomach 1–2; soil 6–7.
Indicator must change near the end point.
NH{{sub:4Cl}} gives acidic; Na{{sub:2CO}}{{sub:3}} gives basic solutions.
content.takeaway: pH counts hydrogen ions, titration counts moles and hydrolysis sets the character.

check.question: A solution has [H{{sup:+}}] = 1×10{{sup:-3}} mol/dm{{sup:3}}. What is its pH?

visual.caption: Base is added until the indicator changes, so the colour change marks exact neutralisation.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In a titration, find the mole ratio first, then the volumes. The ratio decides: 1:1 is a swap, 2:1 halves one side.

The base has twice as many moles as the acid
Then divide those moles by 0.040 dm{{sup:3}}

content.heading: Go deeper: Why conductance follows dissociation
paragraphs: Conductance needs ions to carry charge to the electrodes. A strong acid like HCl dissociates almost completely, so many ions move and conductance is high. A weak acid like ethanoic acid dissociates only partly, so few ions move and conductance stays low at the same concentration.

Dilution makes the contrast sharper: a weak acid dissociates more as it spreads out, so its molar conductance rises on dilution. Strength is about dissociation; concentration is only about amount. A concentrated weak acid can still conduct less than a dilute strong one.
That is the exam link tested: compare two molar solutions, and the stronger acid shows the higher conductance. The degree of dissociation can be read off the conductance ratio directly.
Bases mirror acids: NaOH is strong and conducts well, ammonia solution is weak and conducts poorly although both are bases. Strength, not the acid–base label, sets the ion count.

Common bases feel soapy, turn red litmus blue and neutralise acids to salts, with NaOH in soap and limewater Ca(OH){{sub:2}} in mortar. Ammonia solution serves as a laboratory base and a fertiliser feedstock. Useful salts include ammonium sulphate fertiliser, sodium chloride for food preservation and calcium hydroxide for soil treatment.
bullets: Conductance counts the ions actually present.
Dilution raises the dissociated fraction of a weak acid.
Strength and concentration are different ideas.
Salt uses: ammonium sulphate fertiliser, sodium chloride food preservation and calcium hydroxide soil treatment.

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing the indicator for a titration
paragraphs: An indicator changes colour across a pH range, so it must change close to the end point of the reaction. Methyl orange changes between pH 3.1 and 4.4, phenolphthalein between 8.2 and 10.0 and litmus changes broadly near 7.

A strong acid with a strong base ends near pH 7, so either indicator works. A weak acid with a strong base ends above pH 7, so phenolphthalein is correct and methyl orange would change too early. A strong acid with a weak base ends below pH 7, so methyl orange is correct.

The titration curve shows why: it jumps through the end-point range sharply for strong–strong pairs and more gently for weak pairs. Read the jump and you see why the wrong indicator gives a false end point.
Litmus is a mixture and changes gradually, so it is a poor titration indicator. Methyl orange and phenolphthalein stay the sharp choices, and the curve tells you which one to pick.

AlCl{{sub:3}} (aluminium chloride) hydrolyses acidic because Al{{sup:3+}} pulls hydroxide from water and leaves hydrogen ions: Al{{sup:3+}} + 3H{{sub:2O}} ⇌ Al(OH){{sub:3}} + 3H{{sup:+}}. CH{{sub:3COONa}} (sodium ethanoate) hydrolyses basic because CH{{sub:3COO}}{{sup:-}} takes a proton from water: CH{{sub:3COO}}{{sup:-}} + H{{sub:2O}} ⇌ CH{{sub:3COOH}} + OH{{sup:-}}. The ion from the weak parent therefore decides the pH the indicator must match.
bullets: Methyl orange changes near pH 3–4; phenolphthalein near pH 8–10.
Weak acid + strong base needs phenolphthalein.
Strong acid + weak base needs methyl orange.
The titration curve shows where the jump falls.
AlCl{{sub:3}}: Al{{sup:3+}} + 3H{{sub:2O}} ⇌ Al(OH){{sub:3}} + 3H{{sup:+}} (acidic); CH{{sub:3COONa}}: CH{{sub:3COO}}{{sup:-}} + H{{sub:2O}} ⇌ CH{{sub:3COOH}} + OH{{sup:-}} (basic).
Buffers beyond blood: limed soil, antacid tablets, anti-dandruff shampoos and detergent builders.

visual.caption: The strong–strong curve jumps sharply through pH 7; the indicator must change inside the jump.

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap between basic salt and base
paragraphs: A basic salt is not a base. The label belongs to salts that keep hydroxide inside the crystal: Mg(OH)Cl is the classic case. And a normal salt can give an alkaline solution: Na{{sub:2CO}}{{sub:3}} does, because CO{{sub:3}}{{sup:2-}} pulls a proton from water and leaves OH{{sup:-}} behind. Solution character is decided by the ion that hydrolyses, never by the salt's name.

The same confusion strikes acidic salts. NH{{sub:4Cl}} is not an acid and not an acidic salt; its solution is acidic because the NH{{sub:4}}{{sup:+}} ion releases a proton to water. NaHSO{{sub:4}} is the genuine acidic salt: the sulphate ion itself still holds a replaceable hydrogen.

The exam loves that pair: solution character asked, salt type implied. The safe habit is to name the ion that hydrolyses and write its equation before deciding. CO{{sub:3}}{{sup:2-}} takes a proton from water and leaves OH{{sup:-}}, so the solution turns basic.
That equation is also the answer to the balancing item. Hydrolysis equations balance atoms and charge together, so write the ion first and you rarely write an unbalanced equation in the hall.

Oxides follow their parents: acidic oxides such as CO{{sub:2}} and SO{{sub:2}} react with bases to make salts, basic oxides such as MgO react with acids, and amphoteric oxides such as ZnO and Al{{sub:2O}}{{sub:3}} react with both. Trioxocarbonate(IV) salts such as Na{{sub:2CO}}{{sub:3}} and CaCO{{sub:3}} fizz with dilute acid to release carbon dioxide: CaCO{{sub:3}} + 2HCl → CaCl{{sub:2}} + H{{sub:2O}} + CO{{sub:2}}. The steady bubbles therefore identify a trioxocarbonate(IV) salt.
bullets: A basic salt is not a base in solution.
An acidic salt is not an acid.
Hydrolysis of the ion decides the solution character.
Write the ion equation before choosing the answer.
Acidic oxide + base → salt; basic oxide + acid → salt; trioxocarbonate(IV) salt + acid → CO{{sub:2}} effervescence.

lessons.title: Electrolysis
lessons.objective: Distinguish electrolytes from non-electrolytes, perform Faraday calculations with Q = It, identify suitable electrodes, predict the products at the electrodes for dilute H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}}, aqueous CuSO{{sub:4}}, CuCl{{sub:2}}, dilute and concentrated NaCl, and fused NaCl, state the factors that affect discharge of ions, describe purification of copper and production of aluminium, sodium, oxygen, chlorine and NaOH, use the electrochemical series and electrode potentials for simple calculations, and identify methods of protecting metals from corrosion.

content.heading: Electrolysis
paragraphs: A dull key dipped into an electroplating bath comes out bright, metal already sitting on it. That is electrolysis at work, and this lesson shows you how electricity moves metal from one place to another. It sounds industrial, but the underlying story is just ions in motion.

content.heading: Electrolytes and the cell
paragraphs: An electrolyte is a substance that carries electricity when molten or dissolved, and is broken apart in the process. Sugar water does not conduct, so it is a non-electrolyte. In electrolysis the anode is positive and the cathode negative.

Electrolysis breaks an electrolyte apart with a current. Use inert graphite for CuSO{{sub:4}}, dilute H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}} and fused NaCl; graphite for brine. Reactive copper dissolves at the anode, so it is used only when copper must deposit.

Which ion comes off follows the electrochemical series and the concentration. At the cathode, metal ions and hydrogen compete, and the lower one in the series wins. At the anode, non-metal anions discharge, but concentrated solutions favour the anion over water.
bullets: Electrolyte = conducts molten/dissolved; non-electrolyte never does.
Anode is positive; cathode is negative.
Inert electrodes pass current; reactive electrodes dissolve.
Discharge follows the series and the concentration.
content.takeaway: The electrolyte, the electrodes and the voltage decide what comes off each pole.

check.question: When copper electrodes are used to electrolyse copper(II) chloride solution, what happens at the anode?
check.why: A reactive copper anode dissolves instead of letting chloride ions discharge.

content.heading: Products for the standard electrolytes
paragraphs: Dilute H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}} gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode; water is the electrolyte that reacts. Aqueous CuSO{{sub:4}} gives copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. CuCl{{sub:2}} solution gives copper and chlorine.

Dilute NaCl gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, while concentrated brine gives hydrogen and chlorine. Fused NaCl gives sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode, because no water competes.

First law: mass liberated is proportional to charge, Q = It, where I is in amperes and t in seconds. Second law: for the same Q, masses liberated are proportional to equivalent masses (molar mass ÷ electrons gained). One Faraday (96500 C) discharges one mole of electrons.
bullets: Dilute H{{sub:2SO}}{{sub:4}} gives H{{sub:2}} at cathode, O{{sub:2}} at anode.
Conc. brine gives H{{sub:2}} and Cl{{sub:2}}; fused NaCl gives Na and Cl{{sub:2}}.
Q = It; 1 F = 96500 C discharges 1 mol of electrons.
Electrode statements are half-equations.
content.takeaway: Name the electrolyte and the electrode, then read the products off the series.

visual.caption: Read the electrolyte and the electrode, then the series gives both products.

check.question: Electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution gives which pair of products?
options: Sodium at cathode, chlorine at anode
Hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode
Hydrogen at cathode, oxygen at anode
Sodium at cathode, oxygen at anode
check.why: Water is reduced to hydrogen, and concentrated chloride discharges chlorine.

content.heading: Uses, series and protecting iron
paragraphs: Electrolysis purifies copper: impure copper dissolves at the anode while pure copper deposits at the cathode. Cryolite holds alumina for aluminium; the Downs cell yields sodium from fused NaCl; brine gives Cl{{sub:2}} and NaOH; oxygen comes from water and air.

The electrochemical series, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, predicts reactivity and displacement. A metal higher up displaces a lower one, so zinc displaces iron but not sodium. Standard potentials (E°) rank the same order; E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.

Corrosion is electrochemical: iron rusts where oxygen and water meet the metal. Painting, greasing or oiling blocks air and water, while cathodic protection sacrifices a more reactive metal like zinc. Electroplating coats a base metal with a rust-resistant one.
bullets: Purification: impure anode, pure cathode.
Aluminium from oxide in cryolite; Na from fused NaCl.
A higher metal displaces a lower one.
Iron is protected by paint, grease or a sacrificial metal.
content.takeaway: Electrolysis purifies, extracts and protects, all by choosing the right metal.

check.question: Which method protects iron from rusting by being sacrificed in its place?
options: Coating with a thin grease layer
check.why: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first and spares the iron.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Faraday items: convert the time to seconds first. Five minutes is 300 s, and minute-to-second slips lose the quiet marks.

steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

steps.reason: 0.20 F equals 0.20 × 96500 = 19,300 coulombs.
steps.result: A faraday converts to coulombs by multiplying by 96,500
steps.predictPrompt: How is a faraday expressed in coulombs?

steps.predictPrompt: Can you walk backwards from 0.224 dm{{sup:3}} to 2.0 A?

steps.reason: Q = I x t

hints: First find Q = It in coulombs
Divide by 96500 to get moles of electrons
Halve it for moles of Cu, then multiply by 63.5

content.heading: Go deeper: Why concentrated brine gives chlorine
paragraphs: In dilute NaCl solution the anode discharges oxygen from water because water is present in large amount and oxidises more easily. In concentrated brine the chloride ions crowd the anode, and their concentration lets them win. Discharge is therefore a contest between ions, and concentration tips the balance.

The same contest explains the cathode in fused NaCl. Water is absent, so sodium ions discharge directly. That is the whole logic of the Downs process: melt the salt, remove the water, and the metal itself must discharge.

Oxygen overpotential, the extra voltage beyond the theoretical value, also matters. Discharging oxygen from water needs extra voltage, so in concentrated brine the chloride route needs less. Think in contests, not lists, and you will predict products for unfamiliar electrolytes.

The Hofmann voltameter shows the contest plainly: hydrogen and oxygen collect in a 2:1 ratio from water. The ratio is the stoichiometry made visible, and it confirms the half-equations without any memorisation.

Graphite and platinum are chosen because they conduct yet do not react, so they survive chlorine and oxygen. Copper or other reactive metals would dissolve and contaminate the products. That is why brine and fused-salt cells use graphite, and CuSO{{sub:4}} cells use graphite or platinum.
bullets: Concentrated chloride outcompetes water at the anode.
Fused NaCl leaves sodium no rival at the cathode.
Water oxidation needs extra voltage (overpotential).
Hofmann voltameter gives H{{sub:2}}:O{{sub:2}} in a 2:1 ratio.

content.heading: Go deeper: Purification of copper step by step
paragraphs: Impure copper is cast into thick slabs and hung as the anode in copper(II) sulphate solution. Pure copper is rolled into thin sheets for the cathode. On passing current, copper atoms dissolve from the anode and an equal mass deposits on the cathode.

Copper ions move through the solution, so the number of Cu{{sup:2+}} ions stays constant. Impurities less reactive than copper, like gold and silver, fall off the anode as anode sludge. Impurities more reactive than copper, like zinc, dissolve but do not deposit at the cathode.

The product is 99.99% pure copper, which is why the process is called electrorefining. Resistivity falls sharply with purity, so the copper works well for wires and electrical work where ordinary copper would waste energy as heat.

The same cell proves the series in action. Only copper among the dissolved metals can discharge at the cathode under these conditions, which is why the deposit is pure. Reactivity, not just voltage, decides the outcome.

Half-cell equations write each electrode separately: at the cathode, Cu{{sup:2+}} + 2e{{sup:-}} → Cu; at the anode, 2Cl{{sup:-}} → Cl{{sub:2}} + 2e{{sup:-}} (or 4OH{{sup:-}} → O{{sub:2}} + 2H{{sub:2O}} + 4e{{sup:-}} in dilute solution). Each is a reduction or an oxidation half-reaction; adding the two, with the electrons equal, gives the full ionic equation.
bullets: Impure copper is the anode; pure copper is the cathode.
Copper dissolves and redeposits, keeping Cu{{sup:2+}} constant.
Less reactive impurities fall as sludge; more reactive ones dissolve.
Electrorefining gives 99.99% pure copper.
Cathode: Cu{{sup:2+}} + 2e{{sup:-}} → Cu; anode: 2Cl{{sup:-}} → Cl{{sub:2}} + 2e{{sup:-}}.

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap between cell and electrolysis poles
paragraphs: In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and oxidation happens there; in electrolysis the anode is positive and oxidation still happens there. The electrode label follows the reaction, not the sign: the anode is where oxidation occurs in both devices. Mixing the two rules is the commonest pole error.

The other trap is writing the cell sign on the electrodes of a powered cell. A power supply fixes the cathode as negative and the anode as positive, but the names cathode and anode still mean reduction and oxidation respectively. Signs follow the supply, names follow the reaction.

Corrosion arguments use the same map. In a rusting nail the iron is the anode because it oxidises. Cathodic protection works by attaching a piece whose anode reaction is preferred, so the protective metal is eaten while the iron is spared.
Repeat the one rule, oxidation happens at the anode in both cases, and pole questions stop being memorisation. One rule covers both devices, which is why it is worth learning properly.

A standard electrode potential (E°) is a half-cell value measured against the standard hydrogen electrode. For a cell, E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, where each half-reaction is written as a reduction. Example: E°(Cu{{sup:2+}}/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn{{sup:2+}}/Zn) = −0.76 V, so E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
bullets: The anode is where oxidation happens in any cell.
Signs differ: negative in a cell, positive in electrolysis.
Corrosion makes iron the anode; protection changes the anode.
Oxidation at the anode is the one rule to keep.

lessons.title: Nuclear Chemistry
lessons.objective: Distinguish ordinary chemical reactions from nuclear reactions, differentiate natural from artificial radioactivity, compare the properties of the different types of nuclear radiations, compute half-life, balance simple nuclear equations, and identify the applications of radioactivity.

content.heading: Nuclear Chemistry
paragraphs: A stone in a fire changes colour but stays stone. A few atoms in a hospital machine change into other elements entirely. The first is a chemical reaction; the second is a nuclear reaction, and this lesson explains the difference and what it means for your exam.

content.heading: Chemical change versus nuclear change
paragraphs: An ordinary chemical reaction rearranges electrons and bonds; it never changes one element into another. Burning carbon makes carbon dioxide, but the carbon atoms are still carbon. Chemical reactions happen at the surface of atoms and need relatively little energy.

A nuclear reaction changes the nucleus itself: the protons and neutrons. Radioactive decay does this: an unstable nucleus breaks down, releasing radiation, and the atom becomes a different element. The energy is a million times larger because the nucleus is involved.

Some radioactivity is natural: uranium and radium in rocks have always been radioactive. Artificial radioactivity is made by bombarding stable nuclei with neutrons or particles, producing new radioactive elements in laboratories and reactors.
bullets: Chemical: electrons and bonds move; element stays the same.
Nuclear: the nucleus changes; element becomes another.
Natural radioactivity is in rocks; artificial is made by bombardment.
content.takeaway: Chemical reactions rearrange atoms; nuclear reactions rewrite them.

check.question: Burning carbon to carbon dioxide is a chemical reaction because
options: It releases a large amount of energy
The carbon atoms remain carbon atoms
check.why: Only electrons and bonds move; the carbon atoms stay carbon throughout.

content.heading: The three kinds of radiation
paragraphs: Alpha particles are helium nuclei (2 protons, 2 neutrons) fired out at high speed. They ionise strongly but are stopped by paper, so they are the least penetrating. Beta particles are fast electrons from the nucleus; they pass through paper but are stopped by a metal sheet.

Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves with no mass and no charge, like very energetic light. They pass through the body and are stopped only by dense lead. In increasing order of penetration is alpha, beta, gamma.
A Geiger counter detects all three by the ionisation they cause. Which absorber stops the ray names the radiation: paper alpha, metal beta, lead gamma.
bullets: Alpha = helium nuclei; stopped by paper.
Beta = fast electrons; stopped by metal.
Gamma = waves; stopped by lead; most penetrating.
content.takeaway: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by metal, gamma needs lead.

check.question: Which radiation passes through paper but is stopped by a metal sheet?
check.why: Beta particles are fast electrons that penetrate paper but not metal.

content.heading: Half-life and nuclear equations
paragraphs: Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay. If 800 g becomes 400 g in one half-life and 200 g in the next, the half-life is simply the time between those steps. Each half-life halves the mass again, whatever the starting amount.
Nuclear equations balance both mass number and atomic number. In {{sup:238}}_9{{sub:2U}} → {{sup:4}}_2He + {{sup:234}}_9{{sub:0Th}} the masses 238 = 4 + 234 and the charges 92 = 2 + 90 both balance.

Fusion joins light nuclei into heavier ones, as in the sun: {{sup:2}}_1H + {{sup:3}}_1H → {{sup:4}}_2He + {{sup:1}}_0n. Fission splits a heavy nucleus, as in {{sup:235}}_9{{sub:2U}} + {{sup:1}}_0n → {{sup:139}}_5{{sub:6Ba}} + {{sup:94}}_3{{sub:6Kr}} + 3{{sup:1}}_0n. Applications include medicine (iodine-131), dating (carbon-14) and power generation.
bullets: Half-life: time for half the sample to decay.
Nuclear equations balance mass number and atomic number.
Fusion joins; fission splits. Applications: medicine, dating, power.
content.takeaway: Each half-life halves the sample; nuclear equations balance both numbers.

check.question: A sample of 800 g has a half-life of 5 years. How much remains after 15 years?
check.why: 15 years is 3 half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 g.
